scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Bush dance developed across key historical eras in Australia.
Early European settlers between 1770 and 1850 brought local dance traditions from the United Kingdom, Ireland, and central Europe.
During the gold rush between 1850 and 1860, miners introduced further European dances, including some arriving via the American gold rush.
on_screen: Map: Australia · Oceania
Image — MISSING

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Traditionally danced at woolshed balls, rural gatherings, and social club Bushy Balls, bush dances function as accessible community socials where all dancers execute known figures together.
Certain dances incorporate social play, such as The Ninepins Quadrille (The Drongo), where an unpartnered individual is playfully mocked, and the Heel-Toe Polka, frequently used with children.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Music is primarily provided by a bush band playing tunes rooted in traditional United Kingdom and Irish repertoires, recognisable to UK, Irish, and US session players.
Rhythms include reels, jigs, marches, waltzes, and hornpipes.
Listen for the Fiddle, Piano, Piano accordion, Melodeon.
The pulse is Reel, jig, march, waltz, and hornpipe meters.

Bush dance music is driven by the melodic interplay of fiddle, accordion, concertina, or tin whistle over the rhythmic strumming of guitar or banjo, grounded by bush bass and percussive rattle from the lagerphone. The tunes comprise traditional Irish and British dance melodies played in reel, jig, march, waltz, or hornpipe meters.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Bush dance takes place in relaxed social environments, traditionally woolsheds, rural halls, and social club venues for Bushy Balls.
Unlike colonial dance, which typically calls for period costume, bush dance adheres to relaxed dress codes.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Shirley Andrews and Max Klubal documented dance figures and instructions in publications such as 'Take Your Partners' (1979) and 'Music for Australian Folk Dancing with Instructions' (1979).
The musical group The Bushwackers popularised The Ninepins Quadrille under the name 'The Drongo'.

The tradition distinguishes general bush dance—characterised by relaxed dress and focus on spatial movement over intricate steps—from colonial dance, which features a greater concern for correct footwork, period dress codes, and dances unique to Australia.

Derived from British, Irish, and central European folk dances transported during European settlement and the gold rush, bush dance evolved through Australian pastoral woolshed culture and post-war folk revivals into contemporary social dance forms.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Bush dance is parent of English country dance: Early British settlers brought country dance traditions that shaped Australian longways sets and circle formations.
Bush dance is parent of Irish dance: Provided core musical repertoire and rhythms such as jigs and reels to bush band music.
Bush dance is sibling of Ceilidh: Shares similar social community dance structures, caller formats, and Gaelic folk tunes.
Bush dance is influence of Square dance: Bush dance shares similarities with American square dances where all dancers execute shared steps and change partners.
